name: Hollow Meridian

stars.name: The Curator
stars.notes: Ancient orange dwarf, metal-poor but still burning steadily on the main sequence. Will outlive most stars in the galaxy. Luminosity approximately 8% solar.

planets.name: Index
planets.notes: Hot, airless rock orbiting at 0.08 AU. Surface is unremarkable except for a single monolithic structure on the terminator line—a metallic spire 3.2 km tall, perfectly vertical, composition unknown.

planets.name: Strata
planets.notes: Former habitable world now stripped of its atmosphere. Geological record shows clear evidence of an ocean and biosphere that existed for at least 2 billion years before abrupt termination approximately 1.4 billion years ago.

planets.name: Appendix
planets.notes: Massive barren world with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere. Contains extensive subsurface tunnel networks—some natural lava tubes, others clearly excavated with geometric precision.

planets.name: Marginalia
planets.notes: Frozen outer world. Surface ice contains suspended particulates arranged in repeating patterns visible only under magnification—possibly data storage in a medium designed to survive geological time.

planets.name: Errata
planets.notes: Distant ice world with an eccentric orbit. Albedo varies across the surface in geometric patches, suggesting buried structures beneath the ice sheet. No expeditions have reached this far into the system.

anomalies.name: The Spire of Index
anomalies.notes: Metallic monolith 3.2 km in height, 200 m at base, tapering to 40 m at apex. Composition includes osmium, iridium, and an unidentified crystalline binder. Absorbs all electromagnetic radiation below UV frequencies. Estimated age: at least 4 billion years.

anomalies.name: The Abrupt Termination
anomalies.notes: Strata's biosphere ended simultaneously across the entire planet approximately 1.4 billion years ago. No impact evidence, no volcanic catastrophe, no stellar event. The ocean simply vanished and all biological activity ceased within what appears to be a single century. Cause unknown.

anomalies.name: The Ice Archive
anomalies.notes: Microscopic particulates suspended in ice in repeating crystallographic patterns. Preliminary analysis suggests an information density of approximately 10^18 bits per cubic centimeter. If this is data storage, Marginalia's ice sheet contains more information than all human civilization combined.

asteroid_belts.name: The Redaction
asteroid_belts.notes: Debris belt with an unusual gap pattern—seven distinct cleared lanes of equal width, as if something swept specific orbital paths clean.

stations.name: Meridian Base
stations.location: Surface of Strata, near geological sampling sites
stations.notes: The largest research installation in the system, focused on Strata's extinction event and the tunnel networks on Appendix. Maintains a secondary team studying the Spire of Index via remote observation.

stations.name: Terminus Relay
stations.notes: Communications relay providing data uplink to the broader research network. Doubles as an emergency shelter for Meridian Base personnel.

faction_control.notes: The Compact maintains exclusive research rights under a long-term Exploration Guild charter. Several universities contribute funding and personnel on rotating assignments.

history: First catalogued in 2312 as a metal-poor orange dwarf of astrophysical interest. Planetary survey in 2389 revealed the Spire of Index, triggering immediate reclassification as a xenoarchaeological priority.

The Unified Archaeology Compact established Meridian Base in 2404. Over the following decades, research teams catalogued the extinction event on Strata, the tunnel networks on Appendix, the anomalous ice on Marginalia, and the cleared lanes in the Redaction belt.

The system has become the most studied ancient site accessible to human researchers. Despite over 150 years of continuous investigation, no artifact has been successfully removed from any site—materials either resist extraction or lose their anomalous properties when disturbed.
description: The Hollow Meridian is an ancient orange star presiding over what appears to be the most complete record of a vanished civilization ever discovered. Five worlds, each bearing different evidence of the same builders: a 3.2-kilometer spire on the innermost rock, a biosphere erased overnight on the second, excavated tunnels on the third, a potential data archive frozen in ice on the fourth, and geometric patterns beneath the ice of the fifth. The Curator burns with the patience of a star that has nine billion years of practice, illuminating a system-wide library written in a language no one can read.

What makes the Hollow Meridian extraordinary is not any single artifact but the coherence of the whole. Every planet bears the marks of the same intelligence, working at different scales and in different media but with a consistent aesthetic: geometric precision, exotic materials, and an absolute refusal to leave biological traces. The Abrupt Termination on Strata—an entire biosphere extinguished in a century with no apparent cause—may represent the builders' departure, or their failure, or something else entirely. The Ice Archive on Marginalia, if it truly contains data, could answer every question. No one has been able to read it.

Thirty-four researchers at Meridian Base and a handful of archaeologists scattered across the system carry on the work of understanding a civilization that existed for billions of years and left behind everything except an explanation. The cleared lanes in the Redaction belt suggest traffic patterns. The tunnels on Appendix suggest habitation. The Spire suggests reverence. But the builders themselves are absent, and every artifact resists removal as if the system itself were designed to be visited but never looted. The Hollow Meridian is an open book in a dead language, and the Curator's dim orange light is the only reading lamp.
